title: Discrete MeanFlow: One-Step Generation via Conditional Transition Kernels

paper.title: Discrete MeanFlow: One-Step Generation via Conditional Transition Kernels
paper.abstract:
Abstract MeanFlow enables one-step generation in continuous spaces by learning an average velocity
over a time interval rather than the instantaneous velocity field of flow matching.
However, discrete state spaces do not have smooth trajectories or spatial derivatives,
so the continuous formulation does not directly apply.
We introduce Discrete MeanFlow, which replaces the motion of a point with the transport of probability mass over finite states.
Our key object is the conditional transition kernel
of a continuous-time Markov chain (CTMC), from which we define a mean discrete rate
that measures the average change in transition probability over a time interval.
We prove a Discrete MeanFlow identity that relates this finite-interval rate
to the instantaneous CTMC generator at the endpoint, with the Kolmogorov
forward equation replacing the spatial chain rule of continuous MeanFlow.
Based on this identity, we parameterize the transition kernel directly using a
boundary-by-construction design that guarantees valid probability outputs and exact
boundary conditions without auxiliary losses.
Since the learned kernel is itself a probability
distribution, generation reduces to a single forward pass followed by one categorical
draw meaning no iterative denoising, ODE integration, or multi-step refinement is required.
We validate the framework on exact finite-state Markov chains, where the learned kernel
recovers the analytical ground truth to high precision, and on factorized synthetic
sequence generation tasks with varying alphabet sizes and sequence lengths.

sections.heading: 1 Introduction
sections.text: Generative models based on flow matching ( Lipman et al., 2023 ; Liu, 2022 ) and diffusion ( Ho et al., 2020 ; Song et al., 2021 ) achieve strong results in images, audio, and molecular design, but require many ODE or SDE integration steps at inference. MeanFlow ( Geng et al., 2025a ) reduces this cost in continuous spaces by learning a velocity averaged over a time interval and deriving an identity that connects it to the instantaneous velocity at the endpoint, enabling exact one-step generation. However, MeanFlow cannot be directly applied to discrete state spaces, limiting its use in tasks such as language generation. Unlike continuous data, tokens do not move smoothly from one value to another as there is no continuous trajectory and no spatial derivative with respect to the state. Existing discrete generative models ( Austin et al., 2021 ; Sahoo et al., 2024 ; Lou et al., 2024 ; Campbell et al., 2024 ; Gat et al., 2024 ) instead learn instantaneous jump-rate functions and generate samples by simulating a continuous-time Markov chain (CTMC) over many steps. Thus, one-step generation in discrete spaces remains an open problem. The core idea of this work is that the right object to generalize is not the motion of a state, but the motion of probability mass over states. In a discrete space, points do not move but probabilities do. A CTMC is fully characterized by its transition kernel, which gives the probability of arriving at each state after a given time interval. We define a mean discrete rate from this kernel that measures the average rate at which probability mass redistributes across states over a finite time interval. We derive a Discrete MeanFlow identity that relates this quantity to the instantaneous CTMC generator at the endpoint, using the Kolmogorov forward equation to connect the kernel’s time derivative to the underlying jump dynamics. A key design choice in our parameterization is what we call boundary by construction . The transition kernel must satisfy the condition that if no time elapses, the system stays in its current state. Rather than enforcing this through a penalty term in the loss, we build it into the model architecture where the learned kernel is a mixture between a delta at the current state and a neural network output, with a mixing coefficient that vanishes at zero time interval. This guarantees that the output is always a valid probability distribution, that the boundary condition holds exactly, and that no auxiliary loss or its associated hyperparameter is needed. Generation with our model is immediate as the learned kernel is already a probability distribution over destination states, so sampling requires only a single forward pass followed by one categorical draw. It does not require iterative denoising, an ODE solver, or multi-step refinement. We validate the framework in controlled settings where the ground truth is known. Figure 1 shows the learned kernel for a 3-state ring CTMC alongside the analytical ground truth. The two matrices are visually indistinguishable, with maximum absolute error below 3 × 10 − 3 3\times 10^{-3} . On factorized synthetic sequence tasks with alphabet sizes up to 16 and lengths up to 32, one-step generation achieves per-position total variation distance below 0.03. These results confirm that the Discrete MeanFlow identity is mathematically sound, the parameterization is expressive, and one-step discrete generation is achievable in practice. Figure 1 : Exact kernel recovery on a 3-state ring CTMC. The learned kernel K θ K_{\theta} closely matches the analytical kernel K K , with maximum absolute error below 3 × 10 − 3 3\times 10^{-3} and accurate recovery of the ring’s asymmetric transition structure. Our main contributions are: 1. We introduce Discrete MeanFlow , a finite-state formulation of MeanFlow that replaces continuous state trajectories with probability transport on the simplex, and derive the corresponding identity connecting finite-interval mean transition rates to the instantaneous CTMC generator. 2. We introduce a boundary-by-construction kernel parameterization that guarantees valid probability outputs and exact boundary conditions by design, with no auxiliary losses. 3. We demonstrate one-step discrete generation and validate it on exact CTMCs and synthetic sequence tasks, recovering ground-truth kernels to high precision.

sections.heading: Diffusion and flow matching.
sections.text: Diffusion models ( Sohl-Dickstein et al., 2015 ; Ho et al., 2020 ; Song and Ermon, 2019 ; Song et al., 2021 ) and flow matching ( Lipman et al., 2023 ; Liu, 2022 ) are prominently used for continuous-space generative modeling producing high-quality samples but require many sequential function evaluations at generation time.

sections.heading: One-step generation.
sections.text: Consistency Models ( Song et al., 2023 ; Song and Dhariwal, 2024 ) , Shortcut Models ( Frans et al., 2025 ) , and Inductive Moment Matching ( Zhou et al., 2025 ) reduce sampling to one or few steps by imposing self-consistency constraints on network outputs, but require careful curriculum schedules or additional losses. MeanFlow ( Geng et al., 2025a ) derives a closed-form identity between average and instantaneous velocities, yielding a principled one-step objective that requires no distillation or curriculum. It has since been extended to robotics ( Sheng et al., 2026 ) , reinforcement learning ( Wang et al., 2026 ; Chen et al., 2025 ) , and audio ( Li et al., 2025 ) , with further theoretical analysis ( Geng et al., 2025b ; Zhang et al., 2025 ) . All of these methods operate in continuous Euclidean spaces and do not apply to discrete spaces where velocity fields are undefined.

sections.heading: Generative models in discrete spaces
sections.text: D3PM ( Austin et al., 2021 ) , SEDD ( Lou et al., 2024 ) , and MDLM ( Sahoo et al., 2024 ) extend diffusion to discrete spaces by learning reverse transitions over finite state spaces, while Discrete Flow Matching ( Gat et al., 2024 ; Campbell et al., 2024 ) replaces ODE-based velocity fields with CTMC rate functions trained via the Kolmogorov forward equation allowing flow matching to be adapted to RL with discrete actions ( Khan et al., 2026 ) . These methods have been applied to language modeling ( Sahoo et al., 2024 ; Lou et al., 2024 ) , protein design ( Campbell et al., 2024 ) , and graph generation ( Yiming et al., 2025 ) . All of these methods require many steps during generation and do not support one-step sampling. Our work addresses this gap by learning the transition kernel directly, enabling generation with a single forward pass.

sections.heading: 3 Background
sections.text: This section reviews the continuous foundations our work generalizes, flow matching and MeanFlow, before introducing continuous-time Markov chains as the discrete counterpart. Figure 2 highlights the key contrast where continuous models move points along smooth velocity-driven trajectories, whereas discrete models describe probability mass flowing between states. Figure 2 : Continuous vs. discrete generative dynamics. Continuous flow matching follows smooth trajectories, whereas discrete dynamics redistribute probability mass over finite states using a CTMC transition kernel K r , t ​ ( y , x ) K_{r,t}(y,x) .

sections.heading: 3.1 Flow Matching
sections.text: Flow matching ( Lipman et al., 2023 ; Liu, 2022 ) learns a velocity field that transports a prior distribution to a data distribution. Given data x ∼ p data x\sim p_{\mathrm{data}} and noise ϵ ∼ p prior \epsilon\sim p_{\mathrm{prior}} , a flow path is constructed as z t = ( 1 − t ) ​ x + t ​ ϵ z_{t}=(1-t)x+t\epsilon , with conditional velocity v t = ϵ − x v_{t}=\epsilon-x . Because a given z t z_{t} can arise from many different ( x , ϵ ) (x,\epsilon) pairs, flow matching trains a network v θ v_{\theta} to fit the marginal velocity field v ⁡ ( z t , t ) = 𝔼 ⁡ [ v t ∣ z t ] v(z_{t},t)=\mathbb{E}[v_{t}\mid z_{t}] . Samples are generated by solving the ODE d d ​ t ​ z t = v ⁡ ( z t , t ) \tfrac{d}{dt}z_{t}=v(z_{t},t) from z 1 = ϵ z_{1}=\epsilon to z 0 = x z_{0}=x . Even with straight conditional flows, the marginal velocity field can induce curved trajectories ( Lipman et al., 2023 ) . Coarse discretization then yields inaccurate samples, so standard flow matching requires many ODE solver steps at generation time.

sections.heading: 3.3 Continuous-Time Markov Chains
sections.text: A continuous-time Markov chain (CTMC) ( Norris, 1998 ) on a finite state space 𝒮 \mathcal{S} is specified by a time-dependent generator u t ​ ( y , x ) u_{t}(y,x) , which gives the instantaneous rate at which the process jumps from state x x to state y y . The generator satisfies u t ​ ( y , x ) ≥ 0 u_{t}(y,x)\geq 0 for y ≠ x y\neq x and ∑ y ∈ 𝒮 u t ​ ( y , x ) = 0 \sum_{y\in\mathcal{S}}u_{t}(y,x)=0 , so that each column sums to zero and probability is conserved.

sections.heading: 4 Discrete MeanFlow
sections.text: Extending one-step generation to discrete spaces is not straightforward. Continuous flow matching and MeanFlow rely on three ingredients that do not exist in discrete settings: smooth trajectories through state space, velocity fields that describe motion along those trajectories, and spatial derivatives that appear in the chain rule when differentiating along a flow. A token cannot move smoothly from one value to another, so none of these tools transfer directly. The central challenge lies in determining the appropriate discrete analogue. A naive strategy is to relax discrete states into continuous embeddings and then apply continuous-space methods. However, this discards the underlying discrete structure and reintroduces iterative sampling during generation. Instead, we argue that the correct object to work with is not the motion of a state but the motion of probability mass across states. This shift in perspective, from tracking the trajectory of a point to tracking the evolution of a distribution, is what makes a principled discrete theory possible. Concretely, a continuous-time Markov chain is fully characterized by its transition kernel, which records how probability redistributes over a finite state space between any two times. We show that this kernel admits a mean discrete rate that plays the role of MeanFlow’s average velocity. We further prove that this rate satisfies a closed-form identity derived from the Kolmogorov forward equation, replacing the chain rule and spatial Jacobian used in the continuous setting. Finally, we show that learning the kernel directly enables one-step discrete generation. Each step of this development requires care as the Kolmogorov forward equation is not a spatial chain rule, and its role in the identity is structurally different from the role of ODE dynamics in the continuous MeanFlow identity.

At the boundary t = r t=r , the process has not moved, so K r , r ​ ( y , x ) = δ y , x K_{r,r}(y,x)=\delta_{y,x} . The total change in conditional probability over the interval [ r , t ] [r,t] is therefore K r , t ​ ( y , x ) − δ y , x K_{r,t}(y,x)-\delta_{y,x} . Dividing by the interval length gives the average rate at which probability mass has moved toward state y y : u ¯ ​ ( y , x , r , t ) := K r , t ​ ( y , x ) − δ y , x t − r . \bar{u}(y,x,r,t)\;:=\;\frac{K_{r,t}(y,x)-\delta_{y,x}}{t-r}. (5) This is the mean discrete rate which replaces the average velocity in continuous MeanFlow, and it is a finite-interval description of dynamics, not an instantaneous one (Figure 14 ). sections.heading: Sampling distribution and computational regime.
sections.text: The expectation in Theorem 4.1 is taken over the law of the reference CTMC. Throughout training we therefore draw x t x_{t} from the reference kernel K r , t ​ ( ⋅ , x r ) K_{r,t}(\cdot,x_{r}) , not from the model K θ K_{\theta} . Because the sampling distribution is fixed by the reference dynamics and does not depend on θ \theta , the gradient of ( 14 ) is an unbiased estimator of the gradient of the population loss. sections.text: Algorithm 2 Discrete MeanFlow: One-Step Generation 1: Trained kernel K θ K_{\theta} ; initial state x 0 ∈ 𝒮 x_{0}\in\mathcal{S} 2: 𝐩 ← K θ ​ ( ⋅ , x 0 , 0 , 1 ) \mathbf{p}\leftarrow K_{\theta}(\cdot,x_{0},0,1) ⊳ \triangleright one forward pass 3: X 1 ∼ Categorical ⁡ ( 𝐩 ) X_{1}\sim\mathrm{Categorical}(\mathbf{p}) ⊳ \triangleright one categorical draw 4: return X 1 X_{1} Given a starting state x 0 x_{0} , we evaluate the learned kernel at the full interval ( r , t ) = ( 0 , 1 ) (r,t)=(0,1) to obtain a probability distribution over destination states, and draw a single sample using Algorithm 4.5 . No iterative denoising, ODE solver, or multi-step Markov chain simulation is required. The kernel parameterization guarantees that 𝐩 \mathbf{p} is a valid probability distribution, so sampling needs no projection or renormalization. This one-step property comes from learning the transition kernel rather than the instantaneous generator. Existing discrete diffusion and flow-matching methods learn u t u_{t} and must simulate the CTMC from t = 0 t=0 to t = 1 t=1 . In contrast, our model learns K r , t K_{r,t} directly, which already captures the cumulative effect of the dynamics over the interval, analogous to how MeanFlow’s average velocity captures cumulative displacement without integrating the instantaneous velocity.

sections.heading: 4.6 Factorized Extension to Sequences
sections.text: For sequence generation over product state spaces 𝒮 = 𝒱 D \mathcal{S}=\mathcal{V}^{D} , the full joint kernel K r , t ​ ( y , x ) K_{r,t}(y,x) is intractable, with output dimension | 𝒱 | D |\mathcal{V}|^{D} . We therefore factorize the kernel across positions, K θ ​ ( y , x , r , t ) ≈ ∏ d = 1 D K θ ( d ) ​ ( y d ∣ x , r , t ) , K_{\theta}(y,x,r,t)\;\approx\;\prod_{d=1}^{D}K_{\theta}^{(d)}(y_{d}\mid x,r,t), (16) where each factor predicts a per-position distribution over y d ∈ 𝒱 y_{d}\in\mathcal{V} conditioned on the full input x x . This reduces the output space from | 𝒱 | D |\mathcal{V}|^{D} to D ⋅ | 𝒱 | D\cdot|\mathcal{V}| .

sections.heading: Exact case: independent coordinate dynamics.
sections.text: The factorization ( 16 ) is exact when the generator decomposes coordinate-wise, u t ​ ( y , x ) = ∑ d = 1 D u t ( d ) ​ ( y d , x d ) ​ ∏ d ′ ≠ d δ y d ′ , x d ′ u_{t}(y,x)\;=\;\sum_{d=1}^{D}u_{t}^{(d)}(y_{d},x_{d})\prod_{d^{\prime}\neq d}\delta_{y_{d^{\prime}},x_{d^{\prime}}} so that only one coordinate changes per jump and its rate depends only on ( x d , y d ) (x_{d},y_{d}) . So the joint kernel splits as K r , t ​ ( y , x ) = ∏ d K r , t ( d ) ​ ( y d , x d ) K_{r,t}(y,x)=\prod_{d}K_{r,t}^{(d)}(y_{d},x_{d}) and each per-coordinate mean rate u ¯ ( d ) \bar{u}^{(d)} satisfies its own Discrete MeanFlow identity, u ¯ ( d ) ​ ( y d , x d , r , t ) = 𝔼 ⁡ [ u t ( d ) ​ ( y d , X t ( d ) ) | X r ( d ) = x d ] − ( t − r ) ​ ∂ t u ¯ ( d ) ​ ( y d , x d , r , t ) . \bar{u}^{(d)}(y_{d},x_{d},r,t)\;=\;\mathbb{E}\!\left[u_{t}^{(d)}(y_{d},X_{t}^{(d)})\,\big|\,X_{r}^{(d)}=x_{d}\right]\;-\;(t-r)\,\partial_{t}\bar{u}^{(d)}(y_{d},x_{d},r,t). (17) Independent masking and per-position uniform or absorbing processes all fall in this regime, so the factorized parameterization is lossless for the corruption processes used in our experiments. However, when the rate at which one coordinate changes depends on the values of other coordinates, the joint kernel no longer factorizes and ( 16 ) becomes an approximation. This has three consequences where the approximation error grows as the interval t − r t-r widens within a single step, the model cannot capture coordinates that should change together in a correlated way, and the per-coordinate training target no longer matches the true joint target exactly.

sections.heading: 5.2 Training Objective Analysis
sections.text: The kernel-residual loss derived from the Discrete MeanFlow identity is mathematically correct, but its practical effectiveness depends on the variance of the stochastic training signal. We compare three training objectives on factorized synthetic sequence tasks with vocabulary sizes | 𝒱 | ∈ { 4 , 8 , 16 } |\mathcal{V}|\in\{4,8,16\} and sequence lengths D ∈ { 8 , 16 , 32 } D\in\{8,16,32\} , using both independent and bigram data distributions. sections.text: The kernel-residual (KR) loss trains ∂ t K θ \partial_{t}K_{\theta} to match the instantaneous generator u t ​ ( y , x t ) u_{t}(y,x_{t}) at a single sampled endpoint x t x_{t} , which introduces two sources of high variance. First, masking corruption makes generator entries scale as 1 / ( 1 − t ) 1/(1-t) , diverging as t → 1 t\to 1 . Second, a single x t x_{t} gives a noisy estimate of the conditional expectation 𝔼 ⁡ [ u t ​ ( y , X t ) ∣ X r = x ] \mathbb{E}[u_{t}(y,X_{t})\mid X_{r}=x] in the Discrete MeanFlow identity. In contrast, posterior regression uses the clean token as a bounded, deterministic target that directly supervises each position. Thus, the KR–PR gap reflects estimator variance rather than an architectural limitation: exact kernel recovery confirms that the identity and parameterization are sound, but the naive single-sample estimator yields high-variance gradients. Figure 5 directly quantifies this effect. For each t t , we draw 5000 samples and measure the per-element target variance. The KR target variance grows as 1 / ( 1 − t ) 2 1/(1-t)^{2} , reaching over 1500 × 1500\times the posterior-regression variance at t = 0.99 t=0.99 , while the posterior-regression target variance remains constant. The right panel further shows that the L 2 L_{2} norm of the KR target closely follows the theoretical scaling | 𝒱 | / ( 1 − t ) \sqrt{|\mathcal{V}|}/(1-t) . These results show that the performance gap in Table 1 is driven by target variance, suggesting lower-variance kernel-residual estimators as a natural direction for future work.

sections.heading: 6 Conclusion, Limitations & Future Work
sections.text: We introduced Discrete MeanFlow, a probability-level formulation of MeanFlow for finite state spaces. Our main contribution is the Discrete MeanFlow identity, which connects a finite-interval mean discrete rate to the endpoint CTMC generator. This replaces the smooth trajectories, velocity fields, and spatial derivatives of continuous MeanFlow with conditional transition kernels, probability mass transport, and the Kolmogorov forward equation. Our boundary-by-construction parameterization guarantees valid probabilities and exact boundary conditions without auxiliary losses, outperforming explicit boundary enforcement by 3 3 – 10 × 10\times . On exact finite-state CTMCs, the learned kernels recover analytical ground truth with maximum entrywise error below 1.3 × 10 − 2 1.3\times 10^{-2} , and one-step samples faithfully reproduce the true conditional distributions. On synthetic sequence tasks, we find that the kernel-residual loss is limited by the high variance of the naive single-sample generator estimate, rather than by the identity or parameterization itself. This identifies a clear next step toward scalable one-step discrete generation by developing lower-variance estimators for the kernel-residual objective.

sections.heading: B.1 Compute Resources
sections.text: All experiments were run on a university GPU cluster using NVIDIA Tesla P100 GPUs (12 GB VRAM) and NVIDIA Tesla V100 GPUs (32 GB VRAM). sections.heading: B.2 Exact kernel recovery experiment setup
sections.text: We train on three reference CTMCs whose true transition kernels are available in closed form via matrix exponentiation.

sections.heading: Reference processes.
sections.text: The 2 state symmetric chain has rate λ = 2 \lambda=2 in both directions. The 3 state ring has clockwise rate λ f = 2 \lambda_{f}=2 and counterclockwise rate λ b = 1 \lambda_{b}=1 . The 10 state birth death chain has birth rate b = 1.5 b=1.5 and death rate d = 1.0 d=1.0 with reflecting boundaries. In all cases the initial distribution p 0 p_{0} is uniform over states.

sections.heading: Model architecture.
sections.text: The kernel network is a 4 layer MLP with hidden dimension 128 and GELU activations. The input is the concatenation of a one hot encoding of the starting state x x (dimension | 𝒮 | |\mathcal{S}| ) and sinusoidal embeddings of r r and t t (dimension 32 each), giving a total input dimension of | 𝒮 | + 64 |\mathcal{S}|+64 . The output is a vector of | 𝒮 | |\mathcal{S}| logits passed through a softmax to produce q θ ​ ( y ∣ x , r , t ) q_{\theta}(y\mid x,r,t) . The boundary-by-construction kernel uses the exponential schedule α ( r , t ) = 1 − exp ( − c ⋅ ( t − r ) ) \alpha(r,t)=1-\exp(-c\cdot(t-r)) where c c is set to twice the maximum absolute entry in the reference generator matrix.

sections.heading: Training.
sections.text: We use AdamW with learning rate 3 × 10 − 4 3\times 10^{-4} , weight decay 10 − 5 10^{-5} , and cosine annealing to 1 % 1\% of the initial learning rate. Batch size is 256. Times are sampled as r ∼ Uniform [ 0 , 1 − ϵ ) r\sim\mathrm{Uniform}[0,1-\epsilon) and t ∼ Uniform ⁡ [ r + ϵ , 1 ] t\sim\mathrm{Uniform}[r+\epsilon,1] with ϵ = 0.01 \epsilon=0.01 . Training runs for 15,000 iterations (2 state), 20,000 iterations (3 state), and 30,000 iterations (10 state). Gradients are clipped to a maximum norm of 1.0.

sections.heading: Evaluation.
sections.text: Kernel accuracy is evaluated on a 20 × 20 20\times 20 grid of ( r , t ) (r,t) pairs. For each grid point, we compute the learned kernel K θ ​ ( ⋅ , x , r , t ) K_{\theta}(\cdot,x,r,t) for every starting state x x and compare against the true kernel K r , t K_{r,t} obtained by matrix exponentiation. One-step generation quality is measured by drawing 5,000 samples from K θ ​ ( ⋅ , x 0 , 0 , 1 ) K_{\theta}(\cdot,x_{0},0,1) for each starting state x 0 x_{0} and comparing the empirical distribution against the true conditional K 0 , 1 ​ ( ⋅ , x 0 ) K_{0,1}(\cdot,x_{0}) using total variation distance.

sections.heading: Data sources.
sections.text: We use two synthetic data distributions. Independent categorical draws each position independently from a fixed random per position distribution over | 𝒱 | |\mathcal{V}| tokens, generated once from a Dirichlet prior with concentration 0.1. Bigram chain generates sequences where position d d depends on position d − 1 d-1 through a random transition matrix, also generated once from a Dirichlet prior. Both distributions have known per position marginals, which serve as the ground truth for evaluating generation quality.

sections.heading: Configurations.
sections.text: We evaluate on six configurations combining alphabet sizes | 𝒱 | ∈ { 4 , 8 , 16 } |\mathcal{V}|\in\{4,8,16\} with sequence lengths D ∈ { 8 , 16 , 32 } D\in\{8,16,32\} , using the matched pairs ( 4 , 8 ) (4,8) , ( 8 , 16 ) (8,16) , and ( 16 , 32 ) (16,32) . Each configuration is run with three random seeds (42, 123, 2024) and results are averaged.

sections.heading: Model architecture.
sections.text: The sequence kernel model is a 3 layer Transformer with model dimension 128, 4 attention heads, and GELU activations. Token embeddings have dimension 128 for | 𝒱 | + 1 |\mathcal{V}|+1 tokens (including the MASK token). Learned positional embeddings are added to each position. Time conditioning uses sinusoidal embeddings of r r and t t (dimension 128 each), projected through a linear layer and added to all positions. The output head produces | 𝒱 | + 1 |\mathcal{V}|+1 logits per position. The boundary-by-construction parameterization uses α ⁡ ( r , t ) = ( t − r ) / ( 1 − r + 10 − 6 ) \alpha(r,t)=(t-r)/(1-r+10^{-6}) . Total parameter count is approximately 300K for all configurations. The posterior regression baseline uses the same Transformer backbone with identical parameter count but conditions on a single time variable t t instead of the pair ( r , t ) (r,t) .

sections.heading: Training.
sections.text: All three objectives (KR, PR, KCE) use AdamW with learning rate 3 × 10 − 4 3\times 10^{-4} , weight decay 10 − 5 10^{-5} , and cosine annealing. Batch size is 256 for KR and KCE, and 128 for PR. Training runs for 12,000 iterations (small configurations with | 𝒱 | ⋅ D ≤ 64 |\mathcal{V}|\cdot D\leq 64 ), 15,000 iterations (medium), or 20,000 iterations (large with | 𝒱 | ⋅ D > 256 |\mathcal{V}|\cdot D>256 ). Masking corruption is applied independently per position with masking probability 1 − τ 1-\tau at generation time τ \tau .

sections.heading: Evaluation.
sections.text: One-step generation quality is measured by generating 5,000 sequences from a fully masked input and comparing the per position empirical marginals against the true data marginals using average total variation distance across positions. Token accuracy is the fraction of positions where the generated token matches a fresh clean sample. Cross-entropy is measured against the true per position marginal at each generated token.

sections.heading: B.4 Boundary Ablation Setup
sections.text: The boundary ablation in Figure 4 compares boundary-by-construction against an unconstrained softmax baseline on the 3 state ring CTMC. The unconstrained baseline uses the same MLP architecture but without the α \alpha -mixing and instead adds a boundary penalty λ bdy ​ ∑ x ‖ K θ ​ ( ⋅ , x , r , r ) − δ ⋅ , x ‖ 2 \lambda_{\mathrm{bdy}}\sum_{x}\|K_{\theta}(\cdot,x,r,r)-\delta_{\cdot,x}\|^{2} to the training loss with λ bdy = 10 \lambda_{\mathrm{bdy}}=10 . All other hyperparameters are identical to the exact kernel recovery experiment setup. Results are reported over three seeds.

sections.heading: B.5 Design Ablation Setup
sections.text: The design ablations in Table 2 are run on the 3 state ring CTMC with the same model and training setup as kernel recovery experiments (15,000 iterations, batch size 256). For the ratio ablation, we vary the fraction of training samples where r ≠ t r\neq t from 0% to 100%. At 0%, all samples use r = t r=t (with a small offset ϵ = 0.01 \epsilon=0.01 for numerical stability), which recovers standard instantaneous generator training. At 100%, all samples use independently sampled r < t r<t . For the time sampler ablation, we compare uniform sampling of t t against two logit normal distributions. For logit normal sampling, we draw z ∼ 𝒩 ⁡ ( μ , 1 ) z\sim\mathcal{N}(\mu,1) and set t = σ ⁡ ( z ) t=\sigma(z) where σ \sigma is the sigmoid function. The two variants use μ = 0 \mu=0 and μ = − 0.4 \mu=-0.4 .

sections.heading: B.6 Target Variance Measurement
sections.text: The target variance analysis in Figure 5 uses no trained model. For each value of t t in the set { 0.05 , 0.1 , 0.2 , … , 0.97 , 0.99 } \{0.05,0.1,0.2,\ldots,0.97,0.99\} , we draw 5,000 clean samples from the independent categorical distribution with | 𝒱 | = 8 |\mathcal{V}|=8 and D = 16 D=16 . Each sample is corrupted at time t t using the masking process, and the reverse generator target u t ​ ( y , x t ) u_{t}(y,x_{t}) is evaluated at each masked position. The per element variance is computed across all masked positions in the batch. For comparison, the posterior regression target is the one hot encoding of the clean token, whose variance depends only on the data distribution and is constant in t t .

sections.heading: B.7 Hybrid Loss Sweep Setup
sections.text: The hybrid loss experiments in Figures 11 and 12 train with the combined objective ℒ = ℒ KR + λ ⋅ ℒ CE \mathcal{L}=\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{KR}}+\lambda\cdot\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{CE}} for λ ∈ { 0 , 0.1 , 1 , 10 , ∞ } \lambda\in\{0,0.1,1,10,\infty\} where λ = 0 \lambda=0 is pure kernel-residual and λ = ∞ \lambda=\infty is pure cross-entropy. All other settings match the factorized sequence task experiment setup. Results are reported for one seed per configuration.

sections.heading: B.8 Statistical Significance
sections.text: All main results (Table 1 , Figures 3 , 4 ) are reported as averages over three independent random seeds (42, 123, 2024). Each seed controls both the model initialization and the random sampling of training data and time pairs. For Table 1 , the standard deviation across seeds is small relative to the gap between methods. For example, on the independent ( 8 , 16 ) (8,16) configuration, the kernel-residual TV distance is 0.030 ± 0.003 0.030\pm 0.003 while the posterior regression TV is 0.008 ± 0.001 0.008\pm 0.001 , so the 3.7 × 3.7\times gap is well outside the noise. The kernel-CE and posterior regression results differ by less than 0.001 0.001 in every seed and configuration pair, confirming that they are statistically indistinguishable. For the boundary ablation (Figure 3 ), boundary-by-construction achieves lower error than the explicit boundary loss on every metric and every seed with no overlap between the two distributions. For the design ablations (Table 2 ), the 0% ratio result ( TV = 0.079 ± 0.000 \mathrm{TV}=0.079\pm 0.000 ) is separated from all nonzero ratios ( TV ≤ 0.005 \mathrm{TV}\leq 0.005 ) by more than 15 × 15\times , confirming that the two-time conditioning is essential.

sections.heading: B.10 Software and Libraries
sections.text: All experiments use PyTorch 2.5.1 with CUDA 12.1. Matrix exponentiation for computing ground-truth kernels uses scipy.linalg.expm (SciPy 1.11). Optimization uses the built-in PyTorch AdamW implementation. No external generative modeling libraries are used.

sections.heading: B.11 Broader Impact
sections.text: This work is foundational research on generative modeling in discrete state spaces, validated entirely on synthetic data. It does not introduce new capabilities for generating text, images, or other content that could be misused. If the framework is eventually scaled to real language generation, it would inherit the same risks as existing discrete generative models, including the potential for generating misleading text. We do not foresee any immediate negative societal consequences from the theoretical and experimental contributions presented here.

However, discrete state spaces do not have smooth trajectories or spatial derivatives, so the continuous formulation does not directly apply. We introduce Discrete MeanFlow, which replaces the motion of a point with the transport of probability mass over finite states. Our key object is the conditional transition kernel of a continuous-time Markov chain (CTMC), from which we define a mean discrete rate that measures the average change in transition probability over a time interval. We prove a Discrete MeanFlow identity that relates this finite-interval rate to the instantaneous CTMC generator at the endpoint, with the Kolmogorov forward equation replacing the spatial chain rule of continuous MeanFlow. Based on this identity, we parameterize the transition kernel directly using a boundary-by-construction design that guarantees valid probability outputs and exact boundary conditions without auxiliary losses. Since the learned kernel is itself a probability distribution, generation reduces to a single forward pass followed by one categorical draw meaning no iterative denoising, ODE integration, or multi-step refinement is required. We validate the framework on exact finite-state Markov chains, where the learned kernel recovers the analytical ground truth to high precision, and on factorized synthetic sequence generation tasks with varying alphabet sizes and sequence lengths. 1 Introduction Generative models based on flow matching ( Lipman et al., 2023 ; Liu, 2022 ) and diffusion ( Ho et al., 2020 ; Song et al., 2021 ) achieve strong results in images, audio, and molecular design, but require many ODE or SDE integration steps at inference. MeanFlow ( Geng et al., 2025a ) reduces this cost in continuous spaces by learning a velocity averaged over a time interval and deriving an identity that connects it to the instantaneous velocity at the endpoint, enabling exact one-step generation. However, MeanFlow cannot be directly applied to discrete state spaces, limiting its use in tasks such as language generation. Unlike continuous data, tokens do not move smoothly from one value to another as there is no continuous trajectory and no spatial derivative with respect to the state. Existing discrete generative models ( Austin et al., 2021 ; Sahoo et al., 2024 ; Lou et al., 2024 ; Campbell et al., 2024 ; Gat et al., 2024 ) instead learn instantaneous jump-rate functions and generate samples by simulating a continuous-time Markov chain (CTMC) over many steps. Thus, one-step generation in discrete spaces remains an open problem. The core idea of this work is that the right object to generalize is not the motion of a state, but the motion of probability mass over states. In a discrete space, points do not move but probabilities do. A CTMC is fully characterized by its transition kernel, which gives the probability of arriving at each state after a given time interval. We define a mean discrete rate from this kernel that measures the average rate at which probability mass redistributes across states over a finite time interval. We derive a Discrete MeanFlow identity that relates this quantity to the instantaneous CTMC generator at the endpoint, using the Kolmogorov forward equation to connect the kernel’s time derivative to the underlying jump dynamics. A key design choice in our parameterization is what we call boundary by construction . The transition kernel must satisfy the condition that if no time elapses, the system stays in its current state. Rather than enforcing this through a penalty term in the loss, we build it into the model architecture where the learned kernel is a mixture between a delta at the current state and a neural network output, with a mixing coefficient that vanishes at zero time interval. This guarantees that the output is always a valid probability distribution, that the boundary condition holds exactly, and that no auxiliary loss or its associated hyperparameter is needed. Generation with our model is immediate as the learned kernel is already a probability distribution over destination states, so sampling requires only a single forward pass followed by one categorical draw. It does not require iterative denoising, an ODE solver, or multi-step refinement. We validate the framework in controlled settings where the ground truth is known. Figure 1 shows the learned kernel for a 3-state ring CTMC alongside the analytical ground truth. The two matrices are visually indistinguishable, with maximum absolute error below 3 × 10 − 3 3\times 10^{-3} . On factorized synthetic sequence tasks with alphabet sizes up to 16 and lengths up to 32, one-step generation achieves per-position total variation distance below 0.03. These results confirm that the Discrete MeanFlow identity is mathematically sound, the parameterization is expressive, and one-step discrete generation is achievable in practice. Figure 1 : Exact kernel recovery on a 3-state ring CTMC. The learned kernel K θ K_{\theta} closely matches the analytical kernel K K , with maximum absolute error below 3 × 10 − 3 3\times 10^{-3} and accurate recovery of the ring’s asymmetric transition structure. Our main contributions are: 1. We introduce Discrete MeanFlow , a finite-state formulation of MeanFlow that replaces continuous state trajectories with probability transport on the simplex, and derive the corresponding identity connecting finite-interval mean transition rates to the instantaneous CTMC generator. 2. We introduce a boundary-by-construction kernel parameterization that guarantees valid probability outputs and exact boundary conditions by design, with no auxiliary losses. 3. We demonstrate one-step discrete generation and validate it on exact CTMCs and synthetic sequence tasks, recovering ground-truth kernels to high precision. 2 Related Work Diffusion and flow matching. Diffusion models ( Sohl-Dickstein et al., 2015 ; Ho et al., 2020 ; Song and Ermon, 2019 ; Song et al., 2021 ) and flow matching ( Lipman et al., 2023 ; Liu, 2022 ) are prominently used for continuous-space generative modeling producing high-quality samples but require many sequential function evaluations at generation time. One-step generation. Consistency Models ( Song et al., 2023 ; Song and Dhariwal, 2024 ) , Shortcut Models ( Frans et al., 2025 ) , and Inductive Moment Matching ( Zhou et al., 2025 ) reduce sampling to one or few steps by imposing self-consistency constraints on network outputs, but require careful curriculum schedules or additional losses. MeanFlow ( Geng et al., 2025a ) derives a closed-form identity between average and instantaneous velocities, yielding a principled one-step objective that requires no distillation or curriculum. It has since been extended to robotics ( Sheng et al., 2026 ) , reinforcement learning ( Wang et al., 2026 ; Chen et al., 2025 ) , and audio ( Li et al., 2025 ) , with further theoretical analysis ( Geng et al., 2025b ; Zhang et al., 2025 ) . All of these methods operate in continuous Euclidean spaces and do not apply to discrete spaces where velocity fields are undefined. Generative models in discrete spaces D3PM ( Austin et al., 2021 ) , SEDD ( Lou et al., 2024 ) , and MDLM ( Sahoo et al., 2024 ) extend diffusion to discrete spaces by learning reverse transitions over finite state spaces, while Discrete Flow Matching ( Gat et al., 2024 ; Campbell et al., 2024 ) replaces ODE-based velocity fields with CTMC rate functions trained via the Kolmogorov forward equation allowing flow matching to be adapted to RL with discrete actions ( Khan et al., 2026 ) . These methods have been applied to language modeling ( Sahoo et al., 2024 ; Lou et al., 2024 ) , protein design ( Campbell et al., 2024 ) , and graph generation ( Yiming et al., 2025 ) . All of these methods require many steps during generation and do not support one-step sampling. Our work addresses this gap by learning the transition kernel directly, enabling generation with a single forward pass. 3 Background This section reviews the continuous foundations our work generalizes, flow matching and MeanFlow, before introducing continuous-time Markov chains as the discrete counterpart. Figure 2 highlights the key contrast where continuous models move points along smooth velocity-driven trajectories, whereas discrete models describe probability mass flowing between states. Figure 2 : Continuous vs. discrete generative dynamics. Continuous flow matching follows smooth trajectories, whereas discrete dynamics redistribute probability mass over finite states using a CTMC transition kernel K r , t ​ ( y , x ) K_{r,t}(y,x) . 3.1 Flow Matching Flow matching ( Lipman et al., 2023 ; Liu, 2022 ) learns a velocity field that transports a prior distribution to a data distribution. Given data x ∼ p data x\sim p_{\mathrm{data}} and noise ϵ ∼ p prior \epsilon\sim p_{\mathrm{prior}} , a flow path is constructed as z t = ( 1 − t ) ​ x + t ​ ϵ z_{t}=(1-t)x+t\epsilon , with conditional velocity v t = ϵ − x v_{t}=\epsilon-x . Because a given z t z_{t} can arise from many different ( x , ϵ ) (x,\epsilon) pairs, flow matching trains a network v θ v_{\theta} to fit the marginal velocity field v ⁡ ( z t , t ) = 𝔼 ⁡ [ v t ∣ z t ] v(z_{t},t)=\mathbb{E}[v_{t}\mid z_{t}] . Coarse discretization then yields inaccurate samples, so standard flow matching requires many ODE solver steps at generation time. 3.2 MeanFlow MeanFlow ( Geng et al., 2025a ) replaces the instantaneous velocity with an average velocity over a time interval [ r , t ] [r,t] : u ⁡ ( z t , r , t ) ≜ 1 t − r ​ ∫ r t v ⁡ ( z τ , τ ) ​ 𝑑 τ . u(z_{t},r,t)\;\triangleq\;\frac{1}{t-r}\int_{r}^{t}v(z_{\tau},\tau)\,d\tau. The generator satisfies u t ​ ( y , x ) ≥ 0 u_{t}(y,x)\geq 0 for y ≠ x y\neq x and ∑ y ∈ 𝒮 u t ​ ( y , x ) = 0 \sum_{y\in\mathcal{S}}u_{t}(y,x)=0 , so that each column sums to zero and probability is conserved. Transition kernel The finite-time behavior of a CTMC is captured by the transition kernel K r , t ​ ( y , x ) := ℙ ⁡ ( X t = y ∣ X r = x ) , K_{r,t}(y,x)\;:=\;\mathbb{P}(X_{t}=y\mid X_{r}=x), (3) which gives the probability of being in state y y at time t t given that the process was in state x x at time r r . For each starting state x x , the column K r , t ​ ( ⋅ , x ) K_{r,t}(\cdot,x) is a valid probability distribution. When no time elapses, the process stays put: K r , r ​ ( y , x ) = δ y , x K_{r,r}(y,x)=\delta_{y,x} . The generator and the kernel are linked by the Kolmogorov forward equation ( Lipman et al., 2024 ) : ∂ t K r , t ​ ( y , x ) = ∑ z ∈ 𝒮 u t ​ ( y , z ) ​ K r , t ​ ( z , x ) , K r , r ​ ( y , x ) = δ y , x . \partial_{t}K_{r,t}(y,x)\;=\;\sum_{z\in\mathcal{S}}u_{t}(y,z)\,K_{r,t}(z,x),\hskip 20.00003ptK_{r,r}(y,x)=\delta_{y,x}. (4) This equation describes how conditional probabilities evolve where the rate of change of the probability of being in state y y is the sum over all intermediate states z z of the probability of currently being in z z times the instantaneous rate from z z to y y . The generator u t u_{t} thus plays the role of a velocity field for discrete dynamics, determining how probability mass redistributes across states at each instant. Recent discrete generative models ( Austin et al., 2021 ; Sahoo et al., 2024 ; Lou et al., 2024 ; Gat et al., 2024 ; Campbell et al., 2024 ) learn such a generator and sample by simulating the CTMC over many time steps. Our goal is to avoid this iterative simulation entirely by learning the transition kernel K r , t K_{r,t} directly, just as MeanFlow avoids ODE integration by learning the average velocity u u directly. 4 Discrete MeanFlow Extending one-step generation to discrete spaces is not straightforward. Continuous flow matching and MeanFlow rely on three ingredients that do not exist in discrete settings: smooth trajectories through state space, velocity fields that describe motion along those trajectories, and spatial derivatives that appear in the chain rule when differentiating along a flow. A token cannot move smoothly from one value to another, so none of these tools transfer directly. The central challenge lies in determining the appropriate discrete analogue. A naive strategy is to relax discrete states into continuous embeddings and then apply continuous-space methods. However, this discards the underlying discrete structure and reintroduces iterative sampling during generation. Instead, we argue that the correct object to work with is not the motion of a state but the motion of probability mass across states. This shift in perspective, from tracking the trajectory of a point to tracking the evolution of a distribution, is what makes a principled discrete theory possible. Concretely, a continuous-time Markov chain is fully characterized by its transition kernel, which records how probability redistributes over a finite state space between any two times. We show that this kernel admits a mean discrete rate that plays the role of MeanFlow’s average velocity. We further prove that this rate satisfies a closed-form identity derived from the Kolmogorov forward equation, replacing the chain rule and spatial Jacobian used in the continuous setting. Finally, we show that learning the kernel directly enables one-step discrete generation. Each step of this development requires care as the Kolmogorov forward equation is not a spatial chain rule, and its role in the identity is structurally different from the role of ODE dynamics in the continuous MeanFlow identity. 4.1 Mean Discrete Rate The starting point is the transition kernel K r , t ​ ( y , x ) K_{r,t}(y,x) , which records the probability of arriving at state y y at time t t given that the process started in state x x at time r r . At the boundary t = r t=r , the process has not moved, so K r , r ​ ( y , x ) = δ y , x K_{r,r}(y,x)=\delta_{y,x} . The total change in conditional probability over the interval [ r , t ] [r,t] is therefore K r , t ​ ( y , x ) − δ y , x K_{r,t}(y,x)-\delta_{y,x} . Dividing by the interval length gives the average rate at which probability mass has moved toward state y y : u ¯ ​ ( y , x , r , t ) := K r , t ​ ( y , x ) − δ y , x t − r . \bar{u}(y,x,r,t)\;:=\;\frac{K_{r,t}(y,x)-\delta_{y,x}}{t-r}. (5) This is the mean discrete rate which replaces the average velocity in continuous MeanFlow, and it is a finite-interval description of dynamics, not an instantaneous one (Figure 14 ). The mean discrete rate inherits structure from the kernel it is derived from. Its off-diagonal entries are non-negative (probability of reaching a new state can only increase), its diagonal entry is non-positive (probability of staying decreases), and its column sums to zero (total probability is conserved). Crucially, the kernel can be recovered by inverting the definition: K r , t ​ ( y , x ) = δ y , x + ( t − r ) ​ u ¯ ​ ( y , x , r , t ) K_{r,t}(y,x)=\delta_{y,x}+(t-r)\,\bar{u}(y,x,r,t) , and this reconstruction is automatically a valid probability distribution. 4.2 The Discrete MeanFlow Identity The central result of this work is an identity that connects the mean discrete rate u ¯ ​ ( y , x , r , t ) \bar{u}(y,x,r,t) to the instantaneous generator u t u_{t} of the CTMC. It provides the foundation for the training objective developed in Section 4.4 . Starting point: the kernel form. By Definition 4.1 , the transition kernel admits the decomposition K r , t ​ ( y , x ) = δ y , x + ( t − r ) ​ u ¯ ​ ( y , x , r , t ) , K_{r,t}(y,x)\;=\;\delta_{y,x}\;+\;(t-r)\,\bar{u}(y,x,r,t), (6) Differentiating in the endpoint time.
